summary: This note summarizes the transition of Egypt from Achaemenid rule to Macedonian and then Roman control. It describes Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BC and the founding of the Ptolemaic Kingdom by his former general Ptolemy I Soter. It also covers the Ptolemies' internal and foreign conflicts, the kingdom's decline, and Egypt's final absorption into the Roman Empire after Cleopatra's death.
one_line: Overview of Egypt's shift from Achaemenid rule to Alexander's conquest, the Ptolemaic Kingdom, and Roman provincial status.
key_facts: In 332 BC, Macedonian ruler Alexander the Great conquered Egypt.
Alexander the Great conquered Egypt as he toppled the Achaemenids.
Alexander the Great established the Hellenistic Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt.
The first ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom was Ptolemy I Soter.
Ptolemy I Soter was one of Alexander's former generals.
The Ptolemies had to fight native rebellions.
The Ptolemies were involved in foreign and civil wars.
The wars of the Ptolemies led to the decline of the Ptolemaic Kingdom.
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was finally annexed by Rome.
The death of Cleopatra ended the nominal independence of Egypt.
After Cleopatra's death, Egypt became one of the provinces of the Roman Empire.
